doc.title: Adaptive Script and ECMAScript
doc.paragraph: Adaptive Script's syntax is close to ECMAScript's, and many of its built-in functions have the names of ECMAScript methods, so someone who knows ECMAScript (JavaScript) can read most scripts at once. It is a language of its own, though: the rest of this reference describes it on its own terms, and this page collects where the two are the same and where they differ, to save surprises when coming from ECMAScript.

list.item: var: declare with let or const.

Classes, prototypes, new, delete, and this. Built-in types such as Array, Object, String, Map, and Error are not there; their methods are functions (see Functions named after ECMAScript methods below).
for .. in: walk keys, values, or entries with for .. of.
Generators, user-defined iterators, and asynchronous operations.
Importing modules: share code through qualified variables.
eval: evaluate runs a string as code, and the code can not see or change variables outside it.
A semicolon ends every statement; it is never inserted for you.
An expression on its own is not a statement ('abc'; and x + 1; are errors); a call, an assignment, ++, and -- are statements.
throw takes a message string, then optional data and id clauses, and catch always receives an error object with message, data, id, and errorCode, not the thrown value.
switch is ECMAScript's, plus an optional using function to compare a value with each case.
A function declared : void is a procedure: its call is the void value, not undefined. ECMAScript has no such return type.
Closures capture let and const bindings and parameters, as in ECMAScript.
integer (64 bits, exact) and double are separate data types, and they do not mix: 1 + 1.0 is an error; write to_double(1) + 1.0. 7 / 2 is 3, and an integer divided by zero is an error.
Integer ** is exact; a negative exponent or a result too large for an integer is an error.

Doubles follow IEEE 754's default handling, as ECMAScript's numbers do: 1.0 / 0.0 is Infinity, 0.0 / 0.0 is NaN, and a comparison with NaN is false. #compile strictDouble; makes invalid operations and division by zero errors instead, which ECMAScript has no way to ask for.
As in ECMAScript, -2 ** 2 is a syntax error; write (-2) ** 2 or -(2 ** 2).

The math functions (sqrt, sin, log, hypot, ...) are ECMAScript's Math functions, but take a double only (write to_double(n) for an integer), and hypot needs at least one value (ECMAScript's Math.hypot() is 0). round rounds halves toward positive infinity, as Math.round does.

The compiler literals #pi, #e, #ln2, #ln10, #log2e, #log10e, #sqrt2, and #sqrt1_2 are the Math constants. #doubleMin is the smallest normal double; ECMAScript's Number.MIN_VALUE is the smallest subnormal one, #doubleMinSubnormal. #integerMaxExactDouble is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.
boolean(v) is ECMAScript's Boolean(v) truthiness (boolean("false") is true). string_to_boolean reads boolean text.
A string is Unicode code points, not UTF-16 code units: length, indexes, at, slice, substring, code_point_at, and the padding functions all count code points, so an emoji is one, never two halves.

Every string is NFC normalized, so equal text is always equal: a decomposed e and combining acute accent is the same string as a precomposed é, wherever either came from. normalize takes "NFC" and "NFKC"; "NFD" and "NFKD" are errors, since the result could not be a string. ECMAScript strings are not normalized.
A string never holds U+FEFF (the byte order mark): it is dropped wherever it appears. ECMAScript keeps it as a character.
pad_start and pad_end with an empty fill string, when padding is needed, are an error; ECMAScript returns the value unpadded.
trim, to_upper_case, and to_lower_case use ECMAScript's white space and Unicode full case mapping, the same in every locale.
url_encode and url_decode are encodeURI and decodeURI.
+ does not convert: "a" + 1 is an error; write "a" + to_string(1). ECMAScript converts the number to a string.
Arrays have no holes: an omitted value in an array literal is an undefined entry, and create_array(n, v) is new Array(n).fill(v).
a[i] counts from the start only, as in ECMAScript: a[-1] is undefined; at(a, -1) is the last entry.
push and unshift return the new length, as in ECMAScript.
concat of arrays takes only arrays; write [...a, v] or push(a, v) to add one value.
sort with no compare function orders values as < does, so [10, 9, 1] sorts to [1, 9, 10]; ECMAScript compares them as strings. A compare function may also return a boolean.
includes, index_of, and last_index_of compare by value, so an equal array or object is found; ECMAScript compares objects by identity.
A script function passed to map, filter, reduce, and the like is called with (value, index, array), as in ECMAScript; a built-in function is called with the value alone, so map(a, to_string) works.
Object property names are strings; a number or boolean in brackets is an error, not converted.

section.title: Regular expressions
section.paragraph: Regular expressions are ICU's, in the Perl tradition. ECMAScript keeps some rules for compatibility with its first, ASCII and UTF-16 days, so these give a different answer than ECMAScript, most of them the same answer as Perl and Python:

list.item: \d, \w, and \b are Unicode, as in Perl and Python 3: é is a word character and ٣ is a digit. For ASCII only, write [0-9] or [A-Za-z0-9_].
The i flag uses full Unicode case folding, as Perl does: /strasse/i matches "Straße".

Without the m flag, $ also matches just before a line terminator at the end of the value, as in Perl, Python, and Java: test(/^ab$/, "ab\n") is true. Write \z for the very end (and \Z for the end or just before a final line terminator, as in Perl and Java).
The line terminators are LF, CR, CR LF, U+0085, U+2028, and U+2029, so . does not match U+0085.
[^] is a syntax error. Write [\s\S], or use the s flag.
A lookbehind must have a bounded length.
In a replacement, write $0 for the whole match (ECMAScript $&), ${name} for a named group ($<name>), and \$ for a dollar sign ($$).
There are no g, y, d, or v flags. Use match_all, or the limit of replace, for every match.
ICU also has things ECMAScript does not, such as \A, \z, \Z, the x flag, inline flags (?i), atomic groups (?>...), and possessive quantifiers a*+.

section.title: Functions named after ECMAScript methods
section.paragraph: A function takes what ECMAScript calls the receiver as its first parameter, and x->f(a) calls f(x, a), so a->map(fn) reads as ECMAScript's a.map(fn). Names are snake case. Some that differ more than that:

row.column: a.with(i, v) (with is a reserved word)
s.match(re) without the g flag, s.matchAll(re)
s.replace; a limit of -1 is s.replaceAll

section.paragraph: A match is an _AdaptiveRegexpMatch_ object: its captures[n] is m[n] of ECMAScript's match array and its groups is m.groups. A replacement function is called with that object, instead of ECMAScript's list of groups.
